The tone of the noble DUKE'S speech was.
singularly, calm and resigned, as he reluctantly
counselled his followers to pass the second
reading of the Bill; all of them apparently
aware that the Ballot Bill is the intended
remedy for many existing evils, which it
would not be policy on the part of its most
ardent promoters to publicly mention; and
which, in the course of time, will prove how
shamefully corrupt is the present system of
Parliamentary elections carried on. In time
to come our Members of Parliament will not
represent themselves alone, and unheed the
wishes of the constituency to whioh they are
accredited, but they will, like one or two
honourable exceptions already, echo the voices'
of those who they are, even now, suppose 4 to
represent.
The noble duke has also signified his will-
ingness to do what he could to see that corrupt
voters were punished, by which we should
infer—as the noble duke's opinions of all
Liberal Governments are supposed to be that
they are on a corrupt basis—he would do all
in his power to punish those who supported
the said corrupt management in opposition to
his views and those of his own particular class.
Therefore, we shall be compelled to thank his
grace for proffering his munificent services,
and decline to accept his charitable and con-
siderate aid in helping to lay the foundation
of the greater reform that will inevitably
follow. The noble duke's determination to
assist in removing the evils attending the
adoption of the Ballot by an ancient country
like ours Only creates ironical applause; at
the foresight of his grace in fancying that he
can already see some of the alleged evils
which must attend the "system of secret and
irresponsible voting ;" although it is more
probable that these evils are but mirages of
his grace's excited imagination. Altogether
the policy pursued by the noble duke was the
wisest that could have been acted upon,
though his deprecation of the system was
severe in the extreme, and which was fullY
echoed by the Earl of SHAFTESBURY, who
maintained that the Ballot could never co-
exist ,with the Monarchy, and it would be the
greatest blow to freedom if the Monarchy
ceased to exist, and was replaced, as it must
be, not by a Republic ruled by the beat men
in the country, but by a pure democracy.
The Earl of CA.RNARVON pronounced it to
be "a crude and ill-digested measure, in-
drawn, full of omissions that failed to secure
the country against great fraud and abuses
and evils; it was illogical and full of snares,
pitfalls and delusions;, and was opposed to the
old English plan and principles which, for
good or ill, had so long been practised."
It showed too plainly with what reluctance
that august assembly passed the measure,
first stigmatizing it as an evil, and then in a
docile manner to pass its second reading.
The Government may soon have the pleasure
of congratulating themselves in having at last
accomplished the work of years, and brought
to a close a subject that has been so much
written upon, and also to pass a measure that
has been wanting for nearly half a century,
and desired, promoted, and supported by every
honest, man in Great Britain.
FREDERIC HOLLINS.

articles.title: STRIKE OF LONDON CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE STRIKE OF LONDON
CARPENTERS.

We are glad to announce that an attemEt is
being made to settle this dispute by arbitration.
The masters, at their meeting on Friday, said that
they were willing t,o submit to arbitration the ques-
tions between them and the men as to the hours of
labour and the rate of wages; but, unfortunately,
this scheme of settlement was hampered with
conditions calculated not a little to interefere with
Its success. It was proposed that the arbiters
should be Lord Derby and Lord Salisbury; that
the arrangement should take place only on condi-
tion that those who had gone out on strike
returned to work at once; and that if the men did
not comply with these requirements, they must
prepare to be "looked out" generally throughout
the trade on Monday next. ' From the first it was
sufficiently obvious that certain points in the
masters' programme could not well be accepted
off-hand by the men, and that the gravest mis-
chief might be done if the proposition of the
masters were to be looked upon as an ultimatum.
• Again, the men did not find in the scheme of the
masters any reasonable security, either in point of
time or in point of method, that the arbitration
would be prompt, comprehensive, and based on
the clearest and most indisputable data; yet they
were called upon, under threat of a lock-out, to
continue as they were, possibly for many weeks or
months, until a Court should have been constituted,
and have got its work formally shaped and put
before it—a matter of no trifling labour and
delicacy when such varied interests are involved.
The resolution adopted on Saturday by the work-
ing men's delegates, is based on an approval of the
principle of arbitration, even while it "absolutely
refuses" to accept the conditions on which that
mode of settlement was proposed by the masters.
We were prepared to find the men advancing the
objections we have noted, and probably the em-
ployers did not take their high tone without some
anticipation that the strikers would at least suggest
a middle ground on which, after due discussion,
both parties might meet.

MEETING OF THE MASTER BUILDERS.

At a large meeting of master builders held on
Friday in the Freemasons' Tavern, London, Mr.
Plucknott in the chair, the demands of the men
were fully discussed; and the action of the masters
to be adopted thereon gave rise to much different
opinion. Ultimately the following resolutions
were adopted :-
1. That this meeting is of opinion that it is
advisable for the employers to do all they reason-
ably can to obviate the necessity of a lock-out;
and expresses its willingness to submit the decision
as to hours of labour and rate of wages to the
Marquis of Salisbury and the Earl of Derby, whose
decision shall be biniing on both parties; but this
resolution is upon the express condition that the
workmen now on strike at Mr. Brass's and Messrs.
Jackson and Shaw's works shall, until the arbi-
trators make their award, return to their employ-
ment at the present rate of wages not later than
Wednesday next, the 12th of June.
2. That the builders now assembled agree to
give notice to the men in their employ, that unless
the proposition contained in the first resolution be
accepted, the works and shops belonging to those
builders in the metropolitan district will be closdd
on the 17th of June.
3. That the builders present do constitute
themselves into a society, to be called the Central
Association of Master Builders, the annual sub-
scription of each member to be one guinea. Each
member shall pay towards the extraordinary ex-
penditure now required a rateable contribution for
each person employed in his estoblishment on the
17th of June. That the following gentlemen be
appointed the committee of the Central Associa-
tion of Master Builders, with full power to act in
any way that they may consider conducive to the
interests of the members of the association; and
that the following gentlemen ho the committee,
with power to add to their number: Messrs.
Plucknett, Hannen, S. Bird, Richards, Smith,
Trollope, F. Dove, Brass, Dines, and Jackson.
These resolutions wore ordered to be forwarded
to the workmen.

articles.title: MEETING PF THE DELEGATES.
articles.text:
MEETING PF THE DELEGATES.

On Saturday night a crowded meeting of the
delegates appointed amongst the workmen em-
ployed in the various branches of the building
trade took place at the Brown Bear, High-street,
Bloomsbury, for the purpose of receiving reports
as to the feeling of the men in the different shops,
and to consider the resolutions adopted by the
masters at their meeting on Friday. Mr. Sadler
presided. _ -

The Chairman read the resolution adopted at the
masters' meeting, and which we print above.
The reading of theso resolutions was received
with marks of derision and strong disapprobation.
- Mr. Smith, one of those on strike, in the em-
ploy of Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, said he looked
upon this ultimatum of the masters as most dis-
graceful to working men,--to refer such a matter
to two men like the Marquis of Salisbury and
Earl Derby. What did men who were born with
silver spoons in their mouths know of the wants

Jura- 14,18 n.

of working men? Then they threatened a look-
out of the whole trade if the men out on strike
did not return to their work by Wednesday next.
That is what they say; but did they mean it?
Well, if they did, there was no doubt the weakest
must go to the wall. The masters knew that the
men were organized, and admitted it; but they
felt that they must do something to curry favour
with the public. But how could that be a fair
arbitration which was all one-sided? There were
men of intelligence amongst the workmen, and
why not give them a chance to be arbitrators as
well as these noblemen? The men he represented
were determined to stick out for the nine hours
and 9d. per hour.
A workman said there had been a shop meeting
of Mr. Brass's men that morning, and the 107 men
unanimously ignored the proposal of the musters
to appoint two noblemen to arbitr ate on a question
affecting journeymen carpenters. They would
hear of nothing, if there was to be a reference to
arbitration, unless there should be an equal
number on both sides, with some independent Inall
—an architect—who should be referee and whoa
decision should be binding on both parties. There
was no mistake about Brass's men. They were
determined not to go in again, even if that meeting
of delegates were to say they were to go in. TheY
were determined not to be laughed at bT
masons, but would stick out for the nine hours
and ninepence, and no mistake.
A very large number of proposals WILII sub-
mitted to the meeting as amendments, but the
following was adopted
"That this meeting of delegates hereby ex-
presses its approval of the principle of arbitration
in the settlement of this question. At the saute
time they absolutely refuse to accept the condt-
dons on which it as submitted by the master
builders' meeting."
On this motion being put, it was carried unani-
mously amidst great cheering and exciternent,
taken up by the crowds lining the staircases,
passages, and bar of the house, who were unable
to gain admission to the delegates' room.
After some reports as to personal matters in
reference to some of the firms, and the payment of
money in support of the movement, the proceed*
ings closed at a late hour.

NECIOCIATIONS ENTERED INTO.
On Monday evening, after the Carpenters'
Nine-Hours' Committee had adjourned, Mr.
Matkiu, the secretary, received a note from Mr.
Piper, the Secretary of the Masters' Committee, ,
stating that as the delegates of the men at their'
meeting on Saturday-evening had approved the
principle of arbitration in settling the existing
dispute, the Committee:of Masters were prepared
to meet a deputation on Tuesday at two o'clock to,
settle the terms upon which the arbitration should
be proceeded with. On the strike committee re-
assembling on Tuesday morning the secretart
laid Mr. Piper's letter before them. It was the
unanimous opinion of the committee that before
any deputation could be appointed to meet the
Masters' Committee the delegates must be sum-
mooed to appoint the deputation, and give there
the necessary instructions, the committee haring
no powers to act upon so important a question in=
dependently of the delegates. This opinion was
embodied in a resolution, and having been agreed
to was taken to the Masters' Committee by gr•
Matkin and Mr. Snith, by whom the position of
the committee was explained. After some die"
cussion it was agreed that the meeting should be
held, and that each committee should be repro'
sented by four of its members, with the two sec-
retaries. Upon the return of Messrs. Matkin tiod
Smith, they having reported the result ot their
mission, the committee at once resolved to subrait
the proposal to a meeting of the delegates
Thursday evening. At this meeting the deputation
of four will be appointed and receive their instruo"
tions. A letter was received on Tuesday by the
committee from the firm of Messrs. Hills, organ
builders, stating that the firm, on and after
Saturday next, will concede the nine hours and
the payment of 9d. per hour. Letters to the same
effect were also received from several small firms.

PAYMENT OP TUB MEN ON STRIKE.
The men on strike, to the number of nearly 300,
were paid at noon their strike-pay for the first
week, each man, both society and non-society
men, the latter being far the largest in number,
receiving 245., which left a good balance in the
hands of the treasurer. On Saturday night up-
wards of £250 was paid in by the delegates. In
addition to the 21s. from the Nine Hours COI:
mittee, every society man, "within limits," ifili
receive his strike allowance accorded by the rule'
of his society, which will bring his strike pay 11P
to about the full amount of his wages, had he beon•
at work.
Mr. Mundella, M.P., writes to the Daily Yetcst
thus :—The workmen are ready to arbitrate, but
object to the employers nominating the arbitrators

for both sides. I think the employers must agree
that this objection on the part of the operatives is
not unreasonable. Moreover, should a tribunal,
nominated by the masters only, give a decision
adverse to the men, it would never be accepted
with the same heartiness and satisfaction as one
given by a tribunal constituted of the representa-
tives of both parties. As the two parties are
equally favourable to arbitration, I would re-
spectfully urge upon them to constitute a court of
equal numbers of employers and workmen. Let
their first business be the election of an umpire,
who shall preside over their deliberations and
decide on any point on which they cannot mutually
agree. They will have no difficulty in finding
men of impartial character and sound judgment to
assist them in such a good work. Lord Derby,
Mr. Brassey, M.P., or Mr. Robert Kettle, would
be above suspicion, and would doubtless lend their
good offices if solicited. The latter two gentle-
men would have the great advantage of a technical
acqaintance with the building trades. I hope the
employers will make no difficulty about sitting on
the same Board with their workmen. It is the
surest means of promoting a good understanding
betwixt them, and in each becoming acquainted
with and meeting the difficulties and arguments of
the other. The present moment is one of so much
importance for the building trade, and for the
application of arbitration on sound principles in
present and future disputes, that I venture to
submit these suggestions to the contending parties
through your columns.
The Builder makes a suggestion in order to
prevent the national loss and personal damage and
privation that would result from a lock-out. It
says :—We advise compromise; in other words,
mutual concession. The time at present work°
is 581 hours, at Bd. an hour, bringing 375. Bd. peel
week; the programme asksd for by the men is 51
hours at 9d., or 38s. 3d. a week—an increase
merely of 7d. a week, so far as money gain to the
men is concerned, though entailing a largo in-
crease in the cost of production, at least 12.1 per
cent. as regards the masters. What we propose is
that men and masters should mutually agree to
let the working hours per week be Si (the hours
agreed upon by the engineers), at the rate of 81d.
an hour. This would give exactly the same
money result, 388. 3d., and would more nearly
follow previous progressive improvements.
Whichever side firbt proposes this concession will
secure and deserve the 'sympathy and support of
the outside public. Its joint acceptance would
maintain good feeling, save money, and load to
the avoidance of much sorrowful sacrifice
FRIDAY Mommo.—Last evening the delegates
from the working men's societies, and representa-
tives from the various shops, met at the Brown
Bear, Bloomsbury, to discuss the terms of the
masters' proposal to arbitrate, and the mode of
arranging any proceedings for a settlement of tho
dispute.
Mr. Sadler occupied the chair, and there was a
large attendance of delegates.
The Chairman having road over the correspon-
dence between the masters' and the workmen's com-
mittee, the only addition being that the masters
would meet a deputation from the men on Friday
(to-day), at the Freemasons' Tavern, as they must
lock out on Saturday, unless some terms were
come to.

Along discussion ensued upon the correspon-
dence, and it was ultimately agreed that four
delegates be sent to meet the employers, with the
Secretary. A large number of delegates were pro-
posed, from which the following were selected :
—Messrs. Smith (Jackson and Shaw's shop),
Gurdy (Myers and Son's shop), Sadler (chairman
of delegates), and Sinclair (Myers and Sons shop).
These, with the Secretary, Mr. Maklin, will meet
the masters to-day (Friday) at two o'clock.
The deputation was instructed to insist that the
demands of the men'as embodied in the memorial,
with the code of working rules, be submitted to
arbitration, or if not the deputation to report to
the delegates before agreeing to any terms but
that the men on strike remain out until the dispute
is settled.

From the tone of the meeting it was agreed that
the nine hours must be had under any oireum-
tames.

articles.title: -.---- THE LONDON- TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
-.----
THE LONDON- TRADES COUNCIL.

On Wednesday night a well-attended meeting
of delegates from the Landon Trades societies was
held at the Bell Inn, Old Bailey, for the purpose
of establishing a Trades Council to attend to all
Parliamentary action affecting trades societies,
and generally to protect the interests of those
societies. Upwards of 50 delegates were present,
representing nearly the whole of the principal
trades of the metropolis, and several others were
represented by letter. Mr. George Odger, who
took the chair, said there had a few years since
been a Trades Council in London with limited
powers and influence, and while it existed it had
done much good. From causes unnecessary hero
to detail that Council had ceased all active
operations for some time past, and it had
been thought desirable by many of the
principal trades that a Council should now be
established on a broader basis, embracing every
trade society in the metropolis. It would become
a great power in advancing the social interests of
' the working classes. Hence the present meeting
had been called, and he was glad to see such a
general response from the more important trades.
After some discussion it was unanimously resolved
to establish a London Trades Council, and an
executive committee of 16 delegates was appointed,
with Mr. G. Shipton, painter, as secretary, whose
first duty it will be to prepare a code of rules for
the working of the Council, and to report the same
to an adjourned meeting of delegates.
The chairman then read a letter from Mr.
Frederic Harrison, calling the attention of the
delegates to the Bill introduced into Parliament by
Mr. Vernon Harcourt, having for its object the
amendment of the Criminal Law Amendment Act
as it affected Trades Unions, and which had the
support of a Parliamentary committee of trade
delegates appointed by the Trades Congress lately
hold at Nottingham. Mr. Harrisoa. denounced
the Bill as being worse than the Act it was pro-
posed to amend, and said that opinion was shared
in by Professor Beesly, Mr. 11. Crompton, and
other legal gentlemen. Considerable discussion
ensued in reference to this letter cud the action of
the Trades Parliamentary Committee, and ulti-
mately the following resolution was unanimously
adopted :—"That this meeting, viewing seriously
the differences of opinion existing among the
trade societies regarding the proposed alterations
in the Criminal Law Amendment Act, deems it
necessary, in order to insure a good understanding
between the whole of the societies in the United
Kingdom, to instruct the executive council now
appointed to inquire into and report to a future
delegate meeting the specialities of the provisions
of the proposed amendment Bill of Mr. Harcourt."

articles.title: GLASGOW TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
GLASGOW TRADES COUNCIL.

The weekly meeting of the Glasgow Trades
Council was held en Wednesday, in the Tontine
Hotel, Mr. J. Bennet presiding. A deputation
from tho masons on strike stated that about
800 mon wore out, and 400 had loft the
town in quest of employment, with good
prospects. Besides these, upwards of 1,400 were
working with employers who had conceded the
weekly pays. The Council agreed to give the

articles.title: OLDHAM AMALGAMATED _ TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
THE OLDHAM AMALGAMATED
_ TRADES COUNCIL.

This body hold their quarterly meeting on
Tuesday evening, Juno 11th, at the Bath Hotel.
The president was in the chair, and representatives
from the following trades were present :—Brick
layers, brassfounders, machine-grinders, hatters,
joiners, G.U., painters, skopmakers, spindle and
fly-makers, tailors, tin-plato workers, spinners
(nine branches), card strippers and grinders, prin-
ters, plumbers, cloggers, and the amalgamated
wood turners. _

- _
A spirited discussion arose as to whether any
further steps had been taken in respect to the
disgraceful proceedings.of a certain political clique
at the late:elections. It was decided that the matter
be allowed to drop, the majority of the members
being of the opinion that a discerning public will
be able to measure them according to their true
standard. Some of the members of the Council
stated very distinctly that in consequence of what
had taken place, they should consider themselves
quite at liberty to act very differently at any
future occasion, and they should most assuredly
do it. Some very strong remarks were also made
in regard to the action taken by the President and
Secretary of the Manchester and Salford Truths
Council.

After some other minor business was gone
through, the meeting was brought to a close.

articles.title: BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
THE BUILDING TRADES.

LEEDS MASTER BUILDERS AND TUE OPERATIVE

CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

On Friday evening a conference took place at the
Nag's Head, Upperhead-row, Leeds, between re-
presentatives of the master builders and the opera-
tive carpenters and joiners, in reference to altera-
tions in the working rules. On the part of the
masters there were present Messrs. Thomas
Whiteley (in the chair), Robert Longley, Jabez
Woolley, I. H. Thorp, William Britton, and
Thomas Winn (secretary) ; and, as representing
the men, Messrs. Thomas Inman, Clark Dodds,
John Ilewison, James Johnson, Chris. Best, and
Wm. Knowles. The object of the conference was
to make certain alterations in rules 1 and 2, notice
to this effect having been given in December last.
Rule 1, as it stood before the meeting, was as
follows :

"That all payments be reckoned and paid for
by the hour. That 7d. per hour be the standard
wages of carpenters and joiners. That men work-
ing upon unprotected buildings be paid id. per
hour extra for six weeks before and until six weeks
after Christmas day."
This it was unanimously agreed to alter by
striking out the words after "carpenters and
joiners," and adding "of. fair average ability."
Rule 2, prior to this meeting, stood as follows
"That 50 hours per week be considered a week's
work. That six weeks before and six weeks
alter Christmas, when working in unpro-
tected buildings, the men to start work at seven
a.m. and leave at five p.m. When specified as
above, li hours per day to be taken for meals."
For this it was unanimously agreed to substitute
the following :
"That 50 hours be considered a week's work;
to commenee work at seven a.m. ; to have break-
fast time from half .past eight to nine o'clock, and
dinner-time from half-past 12 to half-past one; to
leave work at half-past five, and on Saturdays at
half-past twelve o'clock; and six weeks before
and six weeks after Christmas, when working in
unprotected buildings, the same rule shall apply
with the exception that the men shall leave work
at five p.m. and be paid for the same time as
those working in the shop."
It will thus be seen that the conference termi-
nated to the satisfaction of both parties.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of the opera-
tive carpenters and joiners of Leeds was held in
the Temperance Hull St. Petr's-street. There
was a largo attendance. The chair was occupied
by Mr. Thomas Inman. The secretary announced
that the working rules agreed upon at the confer-
ence between the masters and the men held last
Friday had been 'received. The meeting unani-
mously approved of the rules, and the ulterations
have thus been settled to the satisfaction of both
masters and men.

articles.title: JOINERS' STRIKE AT HALIFAX.
articles.text:
THE JOINERS' STRIKE AT HALIFAX.

This dispute, which commenced on the Ist
instant, has not terminated. The men require an
advance of is. per week and a reduction of the
hours from fifty-two and a half to fifty. All the
employers have conceded the reduction of hourp,
and seven of them arc willing to give the advance
in wages. There was a full meeting of the em-
ployers on Friday night at the Brown Cow Hotel,
when it was unanimously resorved that as they had
conceded the reduction to 60 hours, they would not
grant the advance in wages. They also resolved
to open their workshops on Monday, when all men
willing to resume work on those terms would receive
employment.

articles.title: LEEDS BRIMLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE LEEDS BRIMLAYERS.

On Friday night a meeting of the operative
bricklayers of Leeds was held at their committee-
room, Ludgate-hill. The Secretary stated that
deputation from the Executive from the Amalga-
mated Society of Bricklayers at Sheffield had
visited Leeds. They stated that out of 104
branches of their society 92 were receiving more
than the Leeds men are standing out for, and so
long as they were refused their demands the
Sheffield Society would support them. The support
will be continued weekly until the termination of
the dispute. At a meeting of the labourers held at
the Bull ar.d Sun on
,Friday evening they also
resolved not to yield the points on which they are
at variance with their employers.

articles.title: TIIE JOINERS' STRIKE AT YORK.
articles.text:
TIIE JOINERS' STRIKE AT YORK.

This strike has been brought to a conclusion.
It commenced on the Ist of March for an advance
of wages and a reduction of the hours from 56 to
50 per week. The men had been receiving 6d. an
hour, and they asked 6id. The employers offered
to reduce the hours of labour to 53 per week, and
to give 60. per hour, which the workmen refused,
and hence the strike., A few days ago six of the
employers met six merulx,rs of the committee of
journeymen at the Friendly Societies' Hall, Cf.stle-
gate, and it was arranged that the men should
work 53 hours per week and receive 61d. per hour.
On these terms the men will resume work on Mon-
day morning.

articles.title: CARPENTERS AND jOINERS OP LEICESTER.
articles.text:
THE CARPENTERS AND jOINERS OP LEICESTER.

A largo meeting of the carpenters and joiners of
Leicester was held on Saturday night in the large
room at the Woodman's Arms, Rutland-street, at
which Mr. Bowles presided. In December last a
movement commenced amongst the several branchts
of the building trade for an advance of wages and
a reduction of the hours for work to nine per day.
A meeting of carpenters was called at the close of
last year, and a committee was then appointed to
manage the matter, and a large number of ncn-
society men joined themselves together to pay
into the hands of this committee subscriptions of
so much per week, for the purpose of meeting the
expenses and allowing as much possible every
week to any carpenter, not in either of the societies
now in existence, who should find it necessary to
strike for what was required. The advance (ld.

Mr. Guile, in the two hundred and fifteenth

BROTTfER MEMBETIS,—In bringing before your
notice the 216th monthly report, we feel a
pleasure in being able to inform you that almost
every branch reports trade as good. Although it

is shown in the tables that there are 46 more on
donation this month than there wero last month,
yet this does not arise from the want. of work, but
is occasioned by some two or three branches seek-
ing an advance of wages, and the employera refusing
to give that advance to all hands. Consequently
some have had to leave their shops through re-
questing that advance, hence the increase upon the
donation fund; and it is hoped that none of our
members will attempt to go and fill the places of
such members who have left their Shops under
these circumstances, unless therobtain the advance
for which their brother members have sacrificed
their shops. It is a question of complete moral
suasion; no strike is involved, each member has
been left to use his own discretion. No member
has been compelled to ask for the advance; but
those who have considered they were entitled to
the advance have had liberty to request it, and not
receiving it, have been alleged such donation as
their date of entrance entitled them to, and we
hope, for the honour of our individual members,
as well as for the society collectively, no member
will go and take his brother's shop, unless he
realizes the advance his brother has requested.
Trade is excellent now; moulders are almost
everywhere wanted, and there is no need that
members should be running here and there for the
purpose of injuring their brother members; let us
leave that to be done by those whose special mission
it seems to be—those Ishmaelitos of society, whose
hands seem to be lifted against every man, and
who would rather make away with their earnings
in debauchery than pay to a society for the pro-
tection of their trade or for the future suzlenta-

A largo body of agricultural labourers,in the,

Until Thursday few persons in Leamington were
probably aware of the existence of a strike among
the agricultural labourers in the adjacent villages

BiLFAST.—The number of mills whose workers
are locked out continues to increase as the notices
expire. White Abbey (spinning and weaving),
Ligoniel (spinning), Ewart's (spinning and
weaving), with about six thousand workers, closed
on Thursday evening—thus leaving about eighteen
thousand persons in alLwithout employment. A
meeting of trade delegates was held on Thursday
night, to organize support for flax-dressers, at
which donations and weekly subscriptions were
promised from other trade societies. Messrs.
Grieves have agreed to give sd. per day advance
in wages, and Id. advance as bonus. Messrs.
Ross, Clonatd Mills, have agreed to an advance
of as. weekly, unconditionally, as have Rolf hill
Spinning Company, and Mr. Hayes, Grove Mill,
and also other millowners in country districts.

Wootwien.—The memorial for the nine hours
limit for the workmen in Woolwich Arsenal was
presented en Saturday. The movement is, how-
ever, not at all general, and a counter memorial,
expressing satisfaction with present arrangements,
is being prepared.
MIDDLETON.—Tho joiners' strike has been
settled by a compromise, the masters agreeing to
give the men 7d. per hoar, which is equivalent to
an advance of 2s. 6d. per week.
MANCIIESTER.—A meeting of the Manchester
and Salford umbrella coverers—women----was
held on Saturday evening at the Crown and
Anchor, Lever-street, for the purpose of forming
a trade society. A committee was formed to
draw up a list of prices to be submitted to the
next general meeting.
SURBlTOL—Following the example of their
sisterhood at Tynemouth, the Washer-women of
Surbiton and another part of Kingston have struck
for higher wages. They demand 6d. more per
day, and fewer hours. On Friday evening they
sent the town crier round to notify that they re-
fused to work unless they were paid 3s. per day
and allowed beer, and thii functionary further
announced that an open air meeting would be
held next week for the purpose of allowing them
to discuss their real or supposed grievances. Last
Monday, when some turned out, they went to
places were others were at work, and compelled
them to leave off.

NowrnantrroN.—The shoemakers' strike at
Northampton, which has lasted for six weeks, is
no nearer a settlement. Mr. Odger has been con-
sulted, and on Friday he addressed the men at
Thrapton, who agreed to co-operate with the men
on strike. After the 20th inst. Northampton will
be blocked against strangers, and society mon will
not be allowed to work for the masters who refuse
the terms asked.

HALIFAX. —On Friday night a very numerous
meeting of carpet weavers was held in the Great
Albion-street School, Halifax, for the purpose of
hearing the reply that had that day been given by
the firm of Messrs. John Crossley and Sons, .Dean
Clough, to the memorial presented a few weeks
ago by a deputation, praying for an advance of
three-eighths of a penny per yard on Brussels
earpettyan equal proportion on other &titles, pay-
ment of day work at the rate of 6d. per hour, and
also for a reduction of the hours to nine per day.
Mr. Richard Goodyear occupied the chair, and
Mr. Charnock, one of the deputation, stated that
the answer to the memorial was that the pro-
prietors would not entertain the question of nine
hours on any consideration, but they bad no
objection to consider "the question of wages.
After some discussion, it was resolved not to press
the nine hours' question for the present, and pre-
pare another memorial confining itself to the
advance of wages.

FRIDAY, JUNE 14, 1872.

THE BUILDERS' STRIKE.

TILE anoieuts had a proverb, that every-
thing unknown may pass for magnificent.
The Masters' Association of London Builders
sought to make themselves imposing by closing
the doors while they deliberated. It has oozild
out, however, that there is nothing so very

formidable in their numbers or. influence.
Strong or weak, they came to see it would be more
politic.to suggest arbitration than to persist in
a lock-out. Perhaps, it was because they
found that the latter measure would be but
partially operative. Anyhow, they came out
with the proposal that the Marquis of Simsn unr
and the Earl of DEBBY should arbitrate in the
dispute. Why two noblemen, two landed
proprietors, two leading members of the Con-
servative party in polities, should. be the
properest men to decide in a question between
master builders and the working artifice's
employed by them is not very obvious to
plain sense. When both arbitrators are
selected by one side, it was not likely
that the difficulty which two judges
not unfrequeutly find in arriving at One
decision would be insuperable. Whoever
may be the arbitrator or the arbitrators,
they ought to be either one or three. If one,
he ought to be an individual accepted by both
parties; if three, one should be chosen by
each
./arty, and the two so appointed, if
, unable to agree, should consent to refer the
matter to the third, an umpire having the
confidence of them both. It is not to be
thought of for a moment, that the two arbitra-
tors should be nominated by the party meeting
a claim with menace, or that they should be
men of noble rarik, of territorial station, and j
committed to the same line of political party;
and that Conservative not Liberal.

When the Masters' Association could make
up their mouths to offer a proposal so pre-
posterous, it was little wonder that they should
have the effrontery to ask the men to return te
work at the old prices and for themold hours ,
until the arbitrators so selected should have
made their award. Far be it from us WIMP'
pose that the two Tory Peers would put off
their decision longer than circumstances might
oblige them. At soonest, however, they would
not have leisure to give their attention
to the subject until the rising of Par-
liament, nor, indeed, without a certain
amount of neeestary recreation. Neither of

the two, we suppose, is much addicted to those
sports of the field, the fore at, and the river, to
which men in their station usually betake
themselves at the end of the session; but they
are made of flesh and blood, which, in all of
that composition, require the mending inflnence
of pure air and active exercise in order to
health and good condition of all the faculties,
bodily,or of the mind.
• But what is the use of talking? The men
are not likely to aocept the Marquis and the
.Earl at the masters' diotation, as has been
sufficiently shown by the names of the two
commoners whom some of them mentioned as
substitutes for them. There will be no arbi-
tration by mutual consent, if the men meet the

proposal of the masters by a proposal the pre-
cise opposite. Both these ideas will have to be
laid, aside, and the two parties, if they are to
come together, must unite upon some one
man, not only not pledged to either, but
occupying a position so neutral and known to
have a disposition so dispassionate, as to contmand equally the respect and confidence of
both,

The master builders do not perhaps in-
tend wrong; they only wish things done in
a way which may lead to wrong. They are
willing to arbitrate the difference between

themselves and their men, only they claim
the right to appoint the arbitrators. The
impartiality and propriety of the proposal is

remarkable. "Heads I win, tail; you lo Ho,"
is a game long usage has not brought into
favour yet.
In arbitration, the very essence of the ,
thing is in the impartial appointment of
the arbitrators. Let that be vitiated, and
the whole thing becomes nought. The curious
part of the matter really is how the em-
ployers did not see the absurdity of the pro-
posal before they made it. They must have
either not meant to arbitrate, or they must
have regarded the men as idiots. The two
noblemen named are no doubt impartial
in en, and would do justice so far as they
saw the way how; but everything connected
with their position, and habitual thinking,
must tend, unconsciously to themselves, to
unfit them for dealing impartially with such
questions as those in dispute betweefl. the
j oiners and carpenters and their employers,

Jun 14, 1872.

For ourselves we are against strikes and
lock-outs. We hold arbitration to be the
only legitimate way of settling trades disputes.
But rather than submit to tribunals unfairly
constituted—rather than countenanee,the cor-
ruption of justice and right at their source—
we should council war to any extremity, and
at any cost. In this matter the men have
acted with spirit and good sense, and if, to the
end, they persevere with like moderation and
fairness, we cannot but believe they will come
triumphantly out of the struggle; but
whether they win or lose, they will certainly
not be disgraced.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS AND
TRADES UNIONISTS.

AT the conference held in London relative
to the strike in the agricultural districts, fear
was expressed by certain parties present lost,
in organizing any committee for the support of
the labourers, the trades union element should
be too strong. At the Leamington conference
which took place since, this apprehension has
produced its legitimate fruit, as, in the consul-
tative:committee appointed by the labourers'
executive, the trades union element has been
nearly altogether left out.
This is to be regretted, but under the cir-
cumstances it is precisely what was to be ex-
pected. And the trades [unionists of the
towns should regard this conduct on the part
of the agricultural labourors and their present
advisers, as no cause for slackening their
efforts to assist the labourers by every means
in their power when the necessity for such
assistance is made known by those who re-
quire it. To do this in the right spirit, it
only requires that a calm review of the whole
situation should be made.

Trades unionism, it must be remembered, is
feared rather than admired by even the most
liberal amongst the middle and upper classes.
It is accepted as a necessity, and, where avail-
able, used by them as a power to further pet
political projects. It is epokeu of openly with
respect, but it is covertly suspected and dis-
liked. They say that where it prevails, and
where the strength it gives to labour is judi-
ciously used, capital is so hold in cheek
that the conditions of labour are rendered more
endurable than they otherwise would be.
Occasionally, too, the attitude of the working
men begets the fear that, some day, labour may
become too strong for capital, and enforce con-
ditions which will seriously interfere with its
accumulation and investment. It is true that
these apprehensions are vague and shadowy,
but for that very reason they are far more
alarming than if they had arisen from a care-
ful study of the actual facts of the case.
It is in this situation of things the agricul-
tural labourers attract public attention by a
demand for inoreaaed wages, and an attempt
to put themselves into union for the purpose of
snore effeetually enforcing that demand. Au
advance in tho wages of agricultural labour is
so clearly a necessity that the instant it was
looked for, everbody admitted its propriety.
Nobody could say that ten or twelve shillings a
week, for an able-bodied man, was, or could
be, anything but disgracefully inadequate as
payment for a week's honest work. By
common consent, therefore, and before con-
sequences could be forecast, the general public
gave a hearty and unqualified assent to the
demands of the labourers for higher wages, and
gave also a tolerably general approval to their
attempts to form unions, for the purpose of
enforcing this demand. Seemly, however,
had this been done, when the newspaper press,
and certain prominent persons amongst those
who had placed themselves openly on
the side of the labourers, raised a
cry of alarm, lest the trades unionists
of the towns should throw themselves
into the contest, and, by so doing, force
on a conflict between the men' and their
employers which might end badly for all
parties, or which, at least, might turn against
the labourers large numbers of people who
would remain on their side, and help them to
fight their battle if they continued to stand
alone.

There is no reason why the trades societies
should regard this outcry otherwise than as
honest and well meant. But, whatever the
spirit in which it is uttered, it should not, for
olle moment, alter their feelings or policy in

reference to the agricultural labourers; nor
should. they think less of their fellow-workers
in the fields because they have been tem-
porarily led astray by it. Mr. Aiwa and those
.who are acting with him on the executive
committee are necessarily but very partially
informed as to the character, influence, and
power of the trade associations. They have
not adequate experience whereby to test the
truth of such statements as may be made to
them by men unfriendly to such organizations.
Suspicion and distrust may be easily excited
in their minds. They have not been in the
habit of relying on each other, or on men
of their own class. They almost necessarily
look up to those above them for help,
for advice, for guidance. They have
only just opened their eyes, and the light,
suddenly admitted, blinds and confuses them.
They are at the commencement of an under-
taking in the carrying out of which they will
need every help they can get. If their unions
are to have in them that power possessed by
unions in the towns they must be permanent,
well-managed, and continually active. In
their present struggle, gentlemen outsiders
may help them, and such aid should be
received gladly and thankfully. But if they
mean to continuo their present work of '
organization, and to get out of it the valu-
able results it is capable of yielding, they
must come to their brother unionists in the
great centres of industry, and get from
them lessons of experience, which other-
wise they may have to pay a price for,
ruinous to themselves and to their cause.
At present everything is now. There is doubt,
diffidence, and confusion, which will give place
to assured confidence and a clearer perception
of rights and duties. Such men as WlLLrait
ALLAN, DANIEL GUILE, and many others,
who have grown old in the management of
trades associations, can give advice which the
best intentioned outsiders cannot possibly have
the moans of communicating. They can in-
form them as to details of organization and
management. They can show them how
prudent it is sometimes to give way to a
pressure rather than entail on themselves the
losses of a useless strike; and how, on the
contrary, to regulate and urge their claims so
as to secure concessions without any disturb-
ance of industry. They will, in fact, be able
to point out to them the value of that general
understanding which springs up in extensive
organizations through the necessity of consider-
ing many interests—an understanding which
includes the employer's success and well-being
—as well as that of the operative—who,
whatever may be said to the contrary, is far
more anxious to rise in prosperity with his
employer than to sink him, or in any way in-
jure him by a too selfish consideration of his
own interests.

It was creditable to the men in union that,
as soon as they understood the agricultural
labourers were on strike, they met together
and forwarded to them funds, that the most
necessitous might be relieved. This was a very
plain duty and it is pleasing to know• that they
sot about its performance as soon as its neces-
sity became known to them. How the
labourers may aot towards them in return is
not a matter of vital importance, nor should it
in any way interfere with them in the doing
of what they believe it right or neeessary to
do.

The working men of the towns are deeply
interested in the success of this movement in
the country. To establish throughout the
length and breadth of the land the spirit and
practice of unionism ;—to foster everywhere
the manly sense of independence that belongs
to it ;—to cultivate unity of thought in
regard to the rights and duties of capital
and labour, and to get everywhere the power of
united notion, is a work which nothing should
cause working men to forego. To be sharers
in a great movement like this, and to be
partakers in its advantages, the agricultural
labourers must, as a matter of necessity, come
to the experienced trades unionists, and now,
as well as at any future time, the men of the
towns should be prepared to receive them with
open arms. The workers of England must
not be two armies, but one, clinging to one
principle, fighting for one cause, with one
spirit, one ,battlo-ory, one great united for-

ward movement. The advancement of labour
is the advancement of the nation, and it is
only in this advancement, and by it, that a
solid foundation of equity in the business of
life can be laid, suitable to the true require-
ments and interests of all classes of the people.
For the artizans of England it should be
enough at present to know that the labourers
in the fields are for the first time partakers of
their thought—soldiers in their great battle;
with time and patience they may be assured
all else must follow.

HR. BASS, M.P., AND SMALL DEBTS.
Mn, BASS'S Bill to abolish plaints in the
County Courts for debts under forty shillings
is not likely to intetest the House of Commons,
whilst it will be sure to call out the hostility
of those tradesmen depending on the poorer
class of customers for support.
There are few worse evils in society than the
indebtedness of the lowest class of working
people for small sums to struggling shop-
keepers. It is a source of perpetual disquiet
and danger to the creditor, as it not only ex-
poses him to serious loss but to those tempta-
tions of adulteration and fraud almost neces-
sary to cover his losses; whilst to the debtor it
is almost beggary. Buying in small retail
quantities, on credit, is almost as certain a
path to ruin as borrowing money on usurious
interest, as in addition to the losses resulting
from overcharge, short weights and measures,
and cheapening adulterations, it cultivates
habits of thoughtless improvidence, which pro-
duce as an almost certain effect, pauperism and
general misery.
Could this one evil be thoroughly eradicated
by any sound legislative measure, the advan-
tages to all parties concerned would be incal-
culable. If they understood their own interests,
the trading community generally would give
Mr. BASS a hearty support in this matter.
The cure is in the hands of traders themselves
if they will use it; but we know they will not
until they are compelled, and no better plan
could well be thought of than to make such
debts irrecoverable in the County Court. The
power to give credit where the individual
case justified it would remain. No tradesman
need refuse any man whose character for
honesty ho is acquainted with, but the man
who gives the credit should do BO wholly on
his own responsibility, and not in the know-
ledge that he has behind him the machinery of
the law to compel repayment at other people's
expense. The working people themselves, who
have gone into co-operation, have abolished
credit as a step essential to their success. They
do millions of pounds sterling per annum for
articles which go for daily consumption into
poor men's houses without giving credit, and
this is found to be an unmixed blessing to the
poor people, who, otherwise, would be liable
to the miseries and losses of a credit system,
and to all the dangers lurking behind it.
Let our readers estimate, if they can, the
misery revealed by the following figures
In 1870 there were 911,735 plaints in the
County Courts of England and Wales, 526,000
of which were for sums between ss. and 405.,
whilst 1,300 were for miserable sums not exceed-
ing ls. But this silly game of " beggar my neigh-
bours" does not end here. Our law shears,
but it also skins; not the wool or the hair,
but the hide and fat also are taken. During
this same period 109,000 executions against
goods for debt were issued, for sums of from
Ss. to 40%, and for sums of Is. to ss. 9,900
executions were issued, whilst, incredible as
it may appear, there were 152 executions for
is. and wider! Let us add to these a few
other figures. Keeping to the twelve months
stated, 6,736 persons were imprisoned for debt,
3,790 of whom were looked up for sums be-
tween ss. and 405., and 37 for debts of 68.
and under. One fact will put the wisdom
with which we deal with small debtors in a
rather strange light. Of 602 prisoners for
debt in Stafford Jail last year, 100 of them
owed an average of 9s. 7d., making in the
aggregate the stun of £47 18s. 4d., which, in
the attempt to recover by imprisonment, cost
in various ways £3OO.
Seriously we may ask whether or not this is
anything but most ridiculous folly as far as
the ends of economy or justice are concerned.
hut it is worse than this when we consider its

evil effects on the poor. Our present system
encourages indebtedness, and then punishes it
in a way ruinous to those who contraot it as
well as to those who give it, We hope
sincerely Mr. BASS will not allow this matter
to drop, as it is by legislation such as he pro-
poses that those sores in our social system can
be cured which almost imperoebtibly sap its
•
vitals.

THE SUPPLEMENTARY ARTICLE.

THE difficulty in the way of a clear under-
standing between America and England is not
overcome. The last hope is in a long post-
ponement. As far as we know, the blame
belongs to the Government at Washington.
President GRANT hangs his hopes of re-election
upon keeping the question open for some time
longer. Mr. GLADSTONE intimates an inten-
tion, without much delay, to lay the whole
correspondence before Parliament. This would
be necessary, if for no other reason, from its
oosing out piecemeal through "the enterprize
of the press." First the Times gets hold of one
portion, and then the Daily News of another.
The latter journal was able to publish a cora-
munieation from Earl GRANVILLE, with Mr.
Fares answer, almost as soon as they bad
passed along the electric wires. Our FOREIGN
SECRETARY proposes a delay of the Ar-
bitration for eight months ; to which
the AMERICAN MINISTER answers, that we
may apply for an adjournment if we
like, but his Government declines having
anything to do with it. They cannot, he
instructs General BOUNCY, directly or in-
directly, be party to an agreement or under-
standing whereby Great Britain is to submit
an argument to the Geneva Tribunal condi-
tionally or under any protest or reservation.
The obligatione of the Treaty are reciprocal,
and no rights are reserved by either Govern-
ment of any qualified action, while the other
is fulfilling the spirit and letter of the Treaty.
If such notice of withdrawal as suggested in
Lord GRANVILLE'S note be given, it will be
the duty of the American Agent and Counsel
to repel it very decidedly and in terms which
self-respect will make necessary. Such notice
would instantly terminate all further nego-
tiations on the part of the United States
Government. Mr. Frsu, in line, will not
oppose the adjournment of the arbitration,
but he will take no part in asking for it.
The situation, therefore, is, that as yet the
two Governments have not been able to agree
upon the terms relating to the conditions of
the future. This is all that, in substance, can
be told; yet gentlemen on all sides are
impatient almost to anger because the PREMIER
can tell them no more. Perhaps it would be
as reasonable to find fault with the journals
that have afforded pieces of information for
not making their revelations perfect and
complete, lacking nothing. Our Govern-
ment, at any rate, are entitled to the
credit of leaving no stone unturned, in
order to save, if possible, a Treaty of the
greatest importance, first to the two English-
speaking nations, and afterwards to all the
world. In eight months from this time, not
only will General GRANT be either re-elected
or relegated to the place of a private citizen,
but the American Congress and the Imperial
Parliament will be again in Session, a fact in
harmony with the natural desire for Parlia-
mentary knowledge of what is taking place in
important negooiations. Delays are always
wearisome, and sometimes dangerous; and
the tone now taken in the two Houses by Lord
CAIRNS and Mr. Dlsitim shows how hard it
is for party feeling to maintain an attitude of
patriotic patience. It is not doing public
service to show distrust, or insinuate treachery,
with respect to the cautious, prudent, and
even slow action of our own Government;
still less, perhaps, to indulge in cen-
sorious comments on the oonduot of
the American treaty-making power. If
nothing more respectable can show us
us the vast importance of that for which Mr.
GLA.DSTONE and his colleagues are earnestly
and laboriously working, surely we see glimpses
of it escaping through the insolent jabber of
Mr. Barnmor, who would have been glad to
hear that the Treaty and everything con-
I aided with it had come to an untimely
end. The right honourable the member
for Buokingliaratablre, he said, had expressed

himself as greatly alarmed at the language'
held by the PaDiE Mrlsna ; but, for ilté
part, ho had been at least as much alarmed at
the proceedings of that gentleman when he
was himself in office. 'There was no ground
for a conflict between the two Sides of the
House on the subject before it, there being
between them what he might term a commu.
nity of error. The original mistake; was the
sanctioning of the principle of arbitration;
and, for that mistake, both sides were equally
responsible. In his opinion, nothing was
more calculated to lower the honour of this
country, or to prejudice its interests, than
sanctioning the principle of arbitration. The
position was one in which a great country
ought riot to be placed. If a country was not so re-
spected, and did not so respect itself as to decide
what was due to its own character and obliga-
tions, it ceased from that mornent to be alreat
country. He understood that there Was likely
to be a considerable delay in theiproseoutien of
the Treaty. He hailed' that announeement
with entire satisfaction, and, he should hear
with still more satisfaction if the Treaty
entirely collapsed.
Than expressions like these—which have, at
least, the merit of sincerity, and speak the
sentiments of a faction by no means yet ex-
tinct—we know of no argument more strong
in favour of sustaining the present Government
in every effort to carry out the admirable
policy which they have declared.

hour last week's issue we 'gave a short
account of the strike of the Huddersfield
and District Postmen, wlitch, to say the least,
was undoubtedly a great mistake—premature,
ill-advised, and conducted without prudence;
while at the same time we do not approve of the
manner in which the whole body of employes
are treated by the "powers. that be." The
employes of all departments in various parts

petitioned the authorities for an increase of

,groaned at on their

dirty business. Of those who volunteqad to

their blindness in voluntarily assisting to take
the bread out of the Mouths of "babes and
sucklings." ,
We observed in our last week's impression
that a 'sufficient number of volunteers could
not be obtained, and the- number had to
be made up by youths. This is not to say that
the ,department could not, if they had. desired
it, find a sufficient number of established letter
carriers who would not volunteer to go, because
it should he borne in mind that the authorities
have power to, and undoubtedly tvou/d, if the
public interest required it, sunonan, viz.
compel men to go; but, at any rate, they need
not go without a respectful protest, and to
send; such men or, even boys to the seat of war
would only be "throwing firebrands among,
the burning," and tend to increase the feeling
of bitterness already existing throughout the
_ _

three kingdoms. The departure of such men
could then only be looked upon by their fellows

The rule which had been obtained to set
aside the action against Alderman Sir R. W.
Carden for an alleged wrongful conviction
was on Tuesday discharged by the Court of
Comtnon Pleas.

Nine mendicants, several of whom had
combined the offence of disorderly and violent
conduct with that of begging, have been dealt
with at the clerkenwell Police-court, and
sentenced to various terms of imprisonment.

At the Marylebone Police-court, on Tues-
day, a labourer named Robert Lee, 30 years of
age, was committed for, trial on a charge of
having wilfully murdered one James-Brown, a
ticket-of-leave man. John Fitzgibbon, who
had been in custody on an accusation of caus-
ing the death of his wife by casting her from
a seoond-floOr window, was released, the
magistrate holding that no jury would convict
upon the evidence which had been brought
before him. At the Thames Court a middle-
aged woman named Tie was remanded on a
charge of attempted suicide, and also with
having endeavoured to drown her son, eleven
years of age.

Carlist deputies crossing the French frontier
have been iuterned, and it is said that Spain
will demand their expulsion from Franco
Some of Martines' band have been disarmed
at the frontier, and sent to Bourges.

A special telegram has been reoeived from
Frankfort on the subject of the persecution
of the Jews in Roumania, which has excited
such lively sympathy in this country. Ac-
cording to this despatch, Lord Granville
acting with the Italian Cabinet, has proposed
to the Governments of Europe the propriety
of holding a Conference on this matter.
Russia, while declining to enter on the CJon-
ference in any way that might re-open the
Eastern question, is prepared to El übsc rib o
joint note addressed to the Government of
Roumania deprecating the outrages complained.
of in the interests of eivilisation. Should
the answer not, be satisfactory, it is added, the
Russian Government "is willing to proceed
in the matter in the 'spirit of the Treaty of
Paris of 1856." Germany responds to the
appeal in substantially the same terms.

Mr. Disraeli spoke at some length on the
occasion of the annual .meeting of the' National
Society for Promoting the Education of the
Poor in the Principles of the Established
Church. The gist of his speech was that the
State had. given up the religious education of
the people, and that the State's deficiency was
the Church's opportunity. The National So-
ciety he had always looked upon as the head-
quarters of the Church of England in the
question of popular education.

Roble College, Oxford, has lost no time in
making its mark in the University. Mr.
Collins, one of its members, has been elocted
to the Pusey and Ellertou Hebrew Scholar-
ship.

At length the dennite fiat has gone forth
against the Jesuits in Germany. A draught
of a bill has been adopted, authorising the
police authorities to forbid members of the
Society 'of Jesus, or a kindred society, residing
in any part of the empire, even if they possess
native rights. Necessary instructions for
carrying out this most unmistakable regula.
tion wiR be forthwith issued by the Federal
Council. ,

street with (meeting a disturbance in the Hay-
market at two o'clock in the morning, were
released by the magistrate, with some season-
able advice as to not frequenting that particu-
lar locality at ouch an hour.

Hotel, Putney, who deposed to witnessing acts
