evidence rebutting his statements was given
by the landlord of the hotel, and by the medical
man who examined the lady in question.

At Asoot the Prinoe of Wales's Stakes were
won by Queen's Messenger, Molly Cobroy
carrying off The Aseet Stakes. The Prince
and Princess of Wales arrived before the be-
ginning of the race with their suite in four
closed carriages, there being an almost in-
cessant, though not violent, rain the whole
day. On leaving for Titness Park the Royal
party wre very warmly cheered. -

From April Ist to the Bth instant the
Treasury receipts amounted to £13,494,150,
an increase of over a million sterling, when
compared with the corresponding period of
last year. The expenditure has been
£12,752,985. The balance in the Bank of
England exceeds eight millions.

Sir Henry Rawlinson as chairman of the
Royal Geographical Society, at a meeting on
Tuesday night, commented upon the telegrams
lately received from Dr. Kirk and Lieutenant
Dawson, and, while failing to see any great
discrepancy between the two, asserted that he
had no doubt that Dr. Livingstone was ydt
alive and making the best of his way to the
sea coast. This announcement was received
with loud cheers.

Germany is looking far into the future with
reference to Alsftee-Lorraine. The" Govern-
ment Bill for deferring the introduction of the
Imperial Constitution until January, 1874,
passed, the qeeond reading. The ground taken
was that these provinces were not yet ripe for
the Federal Constitution in its entirety, and
espeeially that the preliminary ' question of
nationality would have first to be settled.
The Cognoils-General would
_enter on their
functions in the course of the current year.

lit the House of Commons on Tuesday, Mr.
Gladstone made his expected statement as to
the adjournment of the Geneva Arbitration,
going, of necessity, over the same ground as
Lord •Granvine in, the Upper House, but '
adding that the disagreement had been strictly
on the prospective engagement as to indirect
claims in the future, and that there was not
any difference of viewibetween the two Govern-
ments on the course to be taken at Geneva
with respect to the indirect claims under the
Treaty of Washington. He concluded by say-
ing that when a deeision'had been arrived at
as to the postponement it would be the desire
of the Government to lay upon the table the
papers containing the whole of the proceedings.
In reply to a further question, Mr. Gladstone
said that the special term of eight months'
adjournment had been named, as by the time
it had. elapsed the Senate of the 'United States
and the Parliament of this country would be
again in session. Mr. Disraeli after hinting
that the period of eight months had been
fixed on with a view to tiding over the Presi-
dential election declared that he joined issue
with a policy which he believed would 'end in
disaster and disgrace to England. A some-
what angry discussion followed, after which the
House went into committee ,on the Scotch
Education Bill; and, on resuming at nine
o'clock, was (Jaunted out.

A proposal that the religious orders should
be re-established in Spain has been rejected
by the Spanish Senate by 44 votes against 7.

A meetilig of the London Irish Home Rule
Association was held in the Agricultural Hall,
Islington. The chair, was taken by Mr.
O'Ca•vanagh, and atoong those present wore
Messrs. Maguire, Isaac Butt, and Blenner.
assett. Resolutions were unanimously
passed in favour of the prinoiple of Home
Rule, but, at the same time, strongly disavow-
ing any hostile feeling towards England.

A compromise was effected in the romantic
ease of "Gilchrist v. Herbert," which came
before the Lords Justices by way of an appeal
from a decision of• the Master of, the Rolls.
According to the evidence of Mrs. Gilehrist,
her deceased husband, in order to induce her to
become his wife, promised in writing to give
her half of his property. At his death it was
found that he had devised the whole of it to a
daughter by a former wife. The letters in
which the promise was made were not forth-
coming, having been thrown overboard in a
box during a cyclone which happened when
Mrs. Oilohrist was on a voyage to, India.
Evidence Was brought forward, however, of
persons who had seen these letters; and, on
their testimony, the Master of the Rolls raade
a decree declaring the widow entitled to the
moiety she claimed. This was the decision
appealed against; and when it had been heard
the case was stopped by an announcement
that Mrs. Gilchrist had consented to accept a
fourth instead of alalf of her late husband's
property.

A telegram from Darmstadt announces that
the Princess Alice gave birth to a daughter on
Friday.

Mr. R. N. Fowler, M.P., presided over the
annual dinner of the Artists' Benevolent Fund,
on Saturday evening, when subscriptions
amounting to over £6OO were announced. At
the same time the Attorney-General took
the chair at the anniversary festival of the
United Law Clerks' Society,

The Staffordshire Potteries testimonial to
Mr. Bright consists of a cabinet collection of
ceramic art specimens illustrating the industry
of the district. The inscription bears witness
to the right hon. gentleman's "foresight,
eloquence, and faithful character," which
•
have "greatly eoutributed to his country's
prosperity."

News from Mexico has been received in.
New York, stating that Juarez has been de-
feated in a general engagement, and that the
revolutionists are advancing on Matamoras.

It was recently stated in a Vienna paper
that the Emperors of Germany, of Austria,
and of Russia would be present in Nassau on
the 26th instant at the inauguration of a statue
to Baron Stein. A. Berlin telegram, however,
contradicts this announcement. Aecording to
the statement of another paper the King of
Italy will be present at the ceremony, but not
the Czar. In the New Prussian Gazette it is
announced that the Emperor of Austria will
pay a visit to the Emperor of Germany during
the first week of September.

In the Spanish Congress on Monday Senor
Sagasta gave some explanations respecting the
International Society, and stated that the
Powers had requested Sp,ain to draw up a
practicable scheme for opposing the action of
that association. He at the same time blamed
Earl Granville for refusing to adopt repressive
measures against the International.

Several Conservative peers supported the
second reading of the Ballot Bill on Monday
night. Amongst them were the Earl of Bel
-
more, the Earl of Courtown, the Earl .of
Devon, the Earl of Ellesmere' the Earl of
Longford, Earl Nelson, and the Earl of Rosso,
Viscount Bangor, Lords Abinger, Bateman,
Bolton, Chelmsford, Clonourry, Hawke,
Heytesbury, Wharnoliffe, and Zouclie of
Haryngworth. The Liberals who voted against
the Bill were the Duke of Norfolk, the Marquis
of Clanricarde, the Lords Lyttelton, Lyveden,
Stanley of Alderley, and Talbot de Malahide.
The Duke of Richmond, the Earl of Derby,
Earl Russell, the Earl of Shaftesbury, and
Lords Cairns and Westbury did not vote.

'A great grandson of Tippoo Sahib has been
admittod a member of the English bar during
Trinity Term, his intention being to practise
in the Indian courts.

Last week the mortality in London and
twenty other large towns in the United King-
dom was at the rate of 23 deaths annually to
every 1,000 persons estimated. to be living.
In the metropolis, 2,202 births and 1,289
deaths were registered, the former having ex-
ceeded by 51 the average- numbers, while the
latter wore 93 below them. Twenty-seven
persons died from small-pox, 39 from measles,
18 from . scarlet fever, 4 from diphtheria, 63
from whooping-cough, 33 from different farms
of fever (of which 8 were certified as typhus,
18 as enteric or typhoid, and 7 as simple con-
tinued fever), and 24 from diarrho3a. The
fatal oases or fever and diarrhom showed an
increase, while those of the other zymotio
diseases had de,elined. Three deaths from
scarlet foyer were returned. The deaths re-
ferred to diarrho3a, which had been 9 and 15
In the two previous weeks, further rose to 24,
which, however, were 3 below the corrected
average number in the corresponding week of
the last ten years. Two fatal oases of in-
fantile cholera were recorded.

Judgment has been given ia the Galway
election case reserved for the Common Pleas.
Judges Lawson and Morris were in favour of
giving the seat to Captain Trench. Chief
Justice Monahan dissented ; and, Judge Keogh
having explained the reasons for his decision,
the seat was declared to belong to Captain
Trench.

President Grant, in returning thanks for
the marks of confidence and support he has
received, says that, if re-eleeted, he will show
the old zeal and devotion, with the advantage
of added experience in correcting mistakes
inevitable to a novice. When his successor is
elected, "whether this or next term," he hopes
to leave the country in a condition of credit-
able peace at home or abroad.

M. Thiers' threat of resignation unless the
five years' term of service should be carried
caused some momentary consternation; but
the effect has for the time being passed away,
though not without anticipations of a similar
state of things. The Assembly is, however,
forewarned, and therefore forearmed, against
suoh a recurrence. There is, adds a dispatch,
a general disposition to antieipate some striking
political event.

The leading towns in Staffordshire have
recently taken up the weekly hall•holiday
movement with great spirit and success. Since
April there has been an extensive closing of
shops, &0., at 2 o'clock on Fridays at Stoke,
Newcastle-under• Lyme, and Longton ; and at
two on Thursdays at Stone, Penkridge,
Barslein, and Hanley. On the 19th inst. the
tradesmen of Stafford will begin closing their
shops at one on Wednesdays, at which hour
the banks and solicitors' offices will also close.
Clubs for outdoor sports are being rapidly
promoted in connection with the movement.

Marshal Serrano's conduct in reference to
the Carlists, whtch has been so freely can-
vassed of late, was definitely approved by a
formal vote of the Senate on Tuesday.

At Wednesday's sitting of the London'
School Board, a tabular return was presented,
showing that there are 113 schools under the
control of that body, providing accommoda-
tion for more than 30,000 children, and that
in addition eight sites had been purchased for
new schools, for the reception of nearly 7,000
scholars, The Board had further agreed to
purchase 16 sites and had scheduled 13 for
the exercise of their compulsory powers.

The International Four-oared Race was
rowed on Monday evening between Mortlake
and Putney, in the presence of an enormous
number of spectators. The Londoners took
the lead from the beginning, kept the first
plaoe throughout, and won an easy victory.
The time occupied by the contest was 21
minutes 26 seconds, or somewhat less than the
duration of the race of August, 1869, when
the Harvard men were beaten by an Oxford
University crew.

The House of Lords' Select Committee on
the Epping Forest Bill sat on Monday, the Earl
of Stradbroke in the chair. The measure pro-
poses to give the Commissioners appoir4t9d bY
the Act of last year power to stay all legal
proceedings now pending, and to arm them
with the authority of a court of law. The
Bill, after some amendments, was ordered to
be reported to the House.

A meeting on Monday of the general Com-
mittee of the International Prison Congress •
was held in the Adelphi, Sir John Pakingtee,
Bart., M.P., in the chair, to consider the
present position and prospects of the .
proposed Congress to be held in London next
month. The chairman having made some
observations, a report from the Executtve
Committee was read, in which it was statpd
that the Government had declined to appoint
commissioners to the Congress or to grant
peouniary aid, and recommending that the
expenses should be defrayed by public sub-
scription. Sir Walter Crofton, C. 8., moved,
and Mr. Hastings seconded, the adoption of
the report, which was carried. After some
observations from Sir John Bowring, Mr.
Walter Morrison, M.P., and Mr, ,Dickintion,
M.P., it was agreed that the Government
should be asked to grant the use of Burling.-
ton-house for the meeting of the Congress,
and that a subscription list be at once opened.

For a violent assault upon a witness who
had given evidence leading, to the conviction
of several notorious thieves, one of their com-
panions, John Lyons by name, was fined' X 5
by the Marylebone police magistrate, with the
alternative of two months' imprisonment.

Two cases of manslaughter have, been sent
for trial by the Thames police 'magistrate.
In one of these a young man, named Alfred
Clark, employed as a labourer at the London
Hospital, was charged with having caused the
death of another labourer, James Patten by
name. In the other, the prisoner was one
James li'Lavey, a middle-aged man, who was
charged with having killed his wife.

Sunday obstructions in the New-ont caused
another prosecution at tho Southwark Police-
court on Tuesday, when a hawker of fancy
clay pipos was fined 405., with the alternative
of a month's imprisonment.

-Sir Michael Costa had the honour of an
interview with his Royal Highness the Prince
of Wales on Monday, at Marlborough House.
His Royal Highness took the Occasion of pre-
senting to Sir M. Costa a massive gold ring,
bearing an engraved seal of the Royal Albert
Hall, with the inscription inside Pre-
sented by Her Majesty's Commissioners to
Sir Michael Costa, in return for the valuable
services he voluntarily gave upon the occasion
of the opening of the Ilan and of the opening
of the International Eihibition, in 1871."
It will be remembered that the musical ar-
rangements/on the occasions referred to were
under the direction of Sir Michael Costa, who
composed a sacred cantata for the opening of
the Royal Albert Hall.

The Corporation of Penzance, the western-
most town in Cornwall, lately expelled IMO Of
its members for "violent and outrageous
manner and conduct." The aggrieved coun-
cillor applied for a mandamus to compel the
municipal authorities to restore him to his
office, and the Court of Queen's Bench has
granted it on the ground that he had not had
an opportunity of defending himself in every
particular from the charge of obstructing the
public business which had been brought
against him.

On behalf of 11r. William Arthur A'Beekettf
an application was made to the Court of Ex-
chequer, -on Saturday, for an ittachnont
against, the proprietor of the London Figaro
for contempt of court. An action for libel was;
pendia.. ;. hence the form in which the matter .
came afore the judges. The court, while re-
fusing the attachment, warned the defendant
not to continue the • style of writing which.
had given rise to the application for, should
0 he repeated, the result might b 4; different.

A-young man named. Neale pleaded
on Monday, to forging his father's name to a
bond for £ICO. .He had been employed in the
Bengal Civil Service at a salary of £7OO per
annum, and, on returning to England, found
.his income much diminished. Being thus
embarrassed, he determined to go back to
India, and raised £lOO to pay his passage.
His father refusing to become surety for the
• loan the son forged his name, thinking he
should be able to repay the loan on his arrival
• in India. Ho fell ill, after having paid his
passage, and so the fraud was discovered. He
was sentenced by the Recorder to one month's
hard labour.

Thomas Walmsley was charged, at Bow-
street, with the manslaughter of Dennis
Durkin. The affair originated, as usual, in a
beer-house quarrel. The deceased, who was
very drunk, succeeded, notwithstanding the
efforts of the accused to avoid it, in fastening
a quarrel upon him. The result was that the
drunken man was thrown on the flags, and re-
ceived fatal injuries. The prisoner, who. was
a young man, said nothing to the charge, and
was committed for trial.

Op Tuesday evening
.a very large meeting,
at which nearly 3,000 persons were present,
was held in the Church Congress Hall,
Southampton, for the purpose of supporting
the " Claimant " to the Tichborne Estates.
Mr. Alderruan Tucker presided. Mr. Whalley,
M.P., drew attention to the refusal on the part
of the Government to answer the question he
had put in the House respecting the prosecu-
tion of the "Claimant." Mr. Guildford
Onslow, M.P., stated that having placed several
letters of "Roger himself" before the chief
French clerk in the Foreign Office, that gentle-
man had given as his opinion that the writer
had never learnt grammar. The Claimant, in
the course of a lengthy speech, said that Dr.
Wheeler in 1870 saw the Attorney-General,
who asked him whether he (the clamant) was
Arthur Orton; to which he replied he was not.
Dr. Wheeler wrote a letter to the same effect to
Mr. Serjennt Ballantine, but neither the
claimant nor his attorney heard it till just
lately. Before leaving London he heard a
report that Government did not intend to go
on with the prosecution; but he should insist
that they did. ' He should be satisfied with
Mr. Montagu Williams to defend him. If
Government thought they could imprison him
for forty-two days and then quietly withdraw,
they were mistaken. Let the Attorney and
Solicitor-General proceed, and he was ready to
meet them at twenty-four hours' notice.

The commemoration of founders and bene-
factors to the University of Oxford took place
on Wednesday, in the Sheldonian Theatre.
In consequence of disturbances in previous
years, the undergraduates were admitted hi
tickets, which were distributed on condition
of the recipients not interrupting the pro-
ceedings.

The boat in which the English four won the
Anglo-American Boat Race, on Monday, was
placed in the nave of the Crystal Palace on
Tuesday, where it will remain for a few days.
It exemplifies the American apparatus for
steering by the foot, and the sliding seats,
which were adopted on the occasion. It was
built by Clasper, of Oxford, for the London
Rowing, Club, expressly for the International
Boat Race.

A. Nonconformist Conference was held at
Northampton, on Tuesday. It was resolved—
"That this meeting, looking at the whole
subject of education as it now stands, feels
that the only way out of the diffieulties con-
nected with it is the entire separation of
secular from religious instruction in schools
receiving State aid, and therefore pledges it •
self to do all in its power to secure this end."
A local permanent committee was formed to
watch over all matters affeoting the interests
of religious equality, and to eonsult as to the
best method of action, as occasion may arise.

The Grand Prix of Paris was won on
Sunday by Cremorne, the winner of the
Derby. The Grand Prix was established in
1863, through the instrumentality of the Duo
de Morny, the object being to afford an oppor-
tunity for the best animals of both countries
to compete on even terms. Of the nine races
which have since taken place—last year being
a blank—four have been won by English
horses, and the rest by French. Cremorne is
the only English 'horse that has won the
Grand Prix de Paris as well as the English
Derby.

It is stated by the Madras ilthenceum that
the terrible storm which recently did so much
damage in Madras itself was even more de-
structive in its effects at Vellore. Excluding
the military population, which is taken care of
and provided for by the Government, there
are about 5,000 people destitute and homeless.
Moreover, between 700 and 800 persons
perished, while at Madras the loss of life was
small. The distress is very great, and the
Madras Athenwunt says that relief is urgently
needed.

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The directors of the Bank of England
reduced the rate of discount yesterday from
4 per cent, to 31.

Splendid weather was experienced yesterday
at Ascot, when the Prince and Princess of
Wales, with the Duke of Edinburgh, Prince
Arthur, Prince Teck, and the Duke of Cam-
bridge were present. The Gold Cup was Won
by Henri, ridden by Fordhatu ; the favourite,
Favonius, being second, and Hannah third.

A number of the market garden labourers
of Fulham-fields have struck for higher
wages.

A new writ has been ordered to be issued
for the county of Bedford, in the room of Mr.
F. H. Russell, called to the House of Peers.
It is understood that Colonel Stuart will come
forward in the Conservative interest.
A committee has been formed, consisting of
young men from many—of the principal banks,
warehouses, and axes in the City, to raise
funds to place a window in St. Paul's
Cathedral.

The ships composing the Channel squadron
are to rendezvous at Milford, and then pro-
ceed to Holyhead and leave on the 31st inst.
for Liverpool.

With respect to 'the suspension of the linen
manufacture at Belfast, it is said that the
poor-law guardians of that town have resolved
that a deputation of their body should wait
upon the committee of the flaxdressers now on
strike, and afterwards on the employers, with
a view to bring the parties to terms.
About one o'clock yesterday morning a fire
broke out on the premises of Mr. L. Downs,
hatter, 306, High Holborn. The back rooms
on the first, second, third, and fourth floors
were nearly burned out; the stairs from the
first floor wore destroyed, and the back part of
the roof is off; the front rooms and their
contents were seriously damaged by fire. The
loss will fall on the Sun office.

• A Frenchman, aged 45, named Hippolite
Journand, described as a doctor, of 35, Greek-
street, Soho, was given into custody on the
charge of assaulting Mary *Grath and Louisa
Gray, oostermongers. inspector. Crook went
to visit the prisoner in his cell yesterday
morning, and in his presence the prisoner
took-a dose of prussic acid, and died. imme-
diately.
The trial of Margaret Dizblano for the
murder of her mistress, Madame Reil, was
resumed yesterday at the Old Bailey, before
Baron Channell. The court was again
crowded, many of the spectators being ladies.
The prisoner was accommodated with a seat
in the dock, and prior to the commencement
of the prodeedings, held a short conversation
with M. Albert, the interpreter. After some
evidence had been given on behalf of the pro-
secution, Mr. Powell, who did not call any
witnesses, addressed the jury for the prisoner.
The Attorney-General (who was for the pro-
secution) having replied, the trial was ad-
journed.
A public meeting has been bold at Shore-
ditch to protest against the proposed closing of
Sun-street, Bishopagate-street, as a publio
thoroughfare by the Great Eastern Railway
Company.
On the refusal of the King of Spain to
sign certain Bills, involving a suspension of
Constitutional guarantees, the Cabtnet have
resigned. Esparato had been sent for, and in
the event of his refusal to form a Cabinet,
which was thought likely, Cordoba was to. be
called upon.
The policeman charged with burglary in
chambers at Gray's Inn has been sentenced to
five years' penal servitude.
M. de Chilly, the manager at the Odeon
, Theatre at Paris, was seized with an apoplectic
fit at a dinner given by Victor Hugo to the
actors of that establishment, and died upon
being taken home.
Hugh Fay, who has been three tines tried
at the Cavan Assizes 'for the alleged murder
of his sweetheart, the jury on each Occasion
diasgreeiug as to their verdict, was again
brought up in the Court of Queen's Bench,
Dublin, on Wednesday, in order that the
argument might proceed on the motion of the
Crown to have the venue changed to Omagh.
There was a further postponement.
The distribution of prizes and certificates
at the Mill-hill School took place on Wednes-
day. Mr. Baines, M.P., presided, in the
unavoidable absence of Earl Russell.
An authoritative contradiction is given to
the statement that Mr. Bassett, the Liberal
candidate for Bedfordshire, had consented to
stand conditionally on the Marquis of Tavistock
being brought out to contest the county when
he attained his majority.
According to the Poor Law returns, the
total number of paupers last week in the
Metropolis was 106,772, of whom 32,157 were
in workhouses, and 74,615 received outdoor
relief. Compared with the corresponding
week in 1871, 1870, and 1869, those figures
show a decrease of 18,503, 27,324, and 22,945
respectively. The total number of vagrants
relieved was 903,

articles.text:
REVIEWS.

The Technical Educator. Vol. 111. (Cassell,
Petter, and Galpin.)
As a rule, hooks of instruction, of whatever
kind, are perhaps less fitted to promote the
objects of their writers than those belonging
to any other speoial branch of litera-
ture. 'Whether this arises from the fact
that they are undertaken and executed by
incompetent persons--writers naturally un-
fitted for a work requiring so much sympathetic
thoughtfulness—or whether it is that in trying
to simplify their subjects by letting them-
selves clown to the comprehension of young
persons, it is difficult to say. Certain it is,
however, that they usually miss their mark
to the great loss and affliction of the learner.
Works on technical education do not come
quite within the category of ordinary educa-
tional works. To produce a work suit-
able for those who are seeking instructions in
the specialities of trades and professions, so
that each learner seeking information shell
find what he wants, and shall find it stated in
such a manner as to convey clearly to his
mind what he is in search of, must be a task
of great difficulty, and it may be added that
the necessity for such a work is greater even
than its difficulty. If we place our require-
ments fully before us on this head, we shall see
that, as an industrial people, we have a most
extensive range of oecupations—ocoupations
of the highest importance to the welfare of the
nation; occupations which, in fact, are the
source of the superabounding wealth ef the
country,and in which ,unless we excel our rivals
in the skilfulness with which we ply them,
may, nay certainly will, some day, pass into the
hands of others.
There are two conditions of our educa-
tion—or rather want of education—which
tell against us in this matter. First, the
state of general education amongst the
masses of our workers is in a lower condition
in England than in those nations which we
regard as our chief competing rivals. We
have taken steps, however, to put this right,
but in the meantime the danger exists. Next,
our method of instruction in the workshop is
very defective. The old apprenticeship system
has been superseded by a kind of slop teaching
very detrimental to the general run of our
workers. It is true that the old seven-year
apprenticeship system was out of place in
connection with a mechanical power almost
conscious in regard to the operations it
performs; and it is equally true that the
minute division of labour by which our
modern industry is characterised renders it
unnecessary. But, somehow or other, aspeople
usually do, we have passed from one extreme
to the other. In our workshops now the boys
have almost entirely to instruct themselves.
If they give their attention to the business,
so much the better; if they do not, nobody
has much interest in attending to them, as
there is usually so much to be done in our
factories and workshops, that all must look
after themselves. It is not to be wondered at,
therefore, that when young men finish their
short apprenticeships, they have almost
everything of the highest value in their
callings to learn. The mere manipula-
tion they understand and can practice;
but that head work which lightens and speeds
the work of the hand they are not as a rule
capable of in any high degree. If, on com-
menoing as journeyman, a young fellow can
get into a first-class workshop, and is lucky
enough to be placed side by side with a
thoroughly good workman, he will come out
right enough, and when he has thus served as
it were a second term of training, he will be
fit to take his place amongst the best of his
craft.
Now, it is for such persons as these that the
work before us is specially fitted, and it is not
going a hit too far to say that no better book
could be put into the hands of the young men
engaged in the workshops of the country. It
is true that on any one of the many subjects
it handles, books could be found treating the
subject more exhaustively. But, such works,'
it may be said,' are usually high priced, and, as
a matter of course out of the reaoh of work-
ing men. Tiers, however, is a book in every
way well got up.
,Written by men of ability
and experience, not on one, but, on almost
every subject -- a book which as a weekly
or monthly issue is within the reach of the
poorest workman, and which as a volume is
tit for the library shelves of the first men in
the land.
It would be out of place in such a notice as
this even to enumerate the many subjects of
which this admirable volume treats, or to
enumerate the names of the well-known men
of ability who have contributed to its pages.
Enough to say that it treats of nearly every-
thing, and that nearly everything it treats of
is ably handled. And it is right to add that
the illustrations are fully up to the excellence
of the rest of the volume. To our working
readers we can recommend the book for its
practical usefulness; to those who do not live
by labour it is worthy attention for the great
variety of useful information it contains as
well as for the pleasant and instruoitve

The Contemporary Review. (Strahan and
Co.)
The general contents of the present number
of the Contemporary are so excellent that it
would be difficult to overpraise them. The
first article, on "The Religious Education of
Women," is temperate in tone just and dis-
criminating in spirit, and altogether admi-
rable in its propriety and truthfulness. The
writer (the Rev. R. F. Littledale) keeps clear
of all common-place controversy as to women,
in regard to their faculties and rights. He
properly regards them as they are, and criti-
cisms their character and influence on religious
thought and teaching- with great calmness
and accuracy. There is not in this essay, from
the beginniug to the. end, one word of cant,
and that, where the character and conduct of
women have to be discussed, is a very high
recommendation. The whole thing is,
in fact, manly and courageous, but at
the same time temperate and forcible.
We might multiply quotations from this
remarkable article, but we prefer directing
the attention of the reader to it that it may
be enjoyed in its completeness. Mere frag-
ments could not convey any adequate idea of
the excellency of the whole. , The second
article on " 'rho Belief in Immortality," from
the pen of Mr. Fairbairn, is also excellent of its
kind, and will amply repay thoughtful perusal,
though we rather fear that the subject, not-
withstanding its importance, will not prove
attractive te readers who, in the present day,
prefer less serious subjeeta, and above all things
require that they should be treated with that
kind of light superficiality which renders them
easy to understand. An article on "Irish
Charaoter " is well worth reading; the
writer, though not quite correct on all
points, yet possesses a good understanding
of his subject, and this is more than can
usually be said of those who undertake to deal
with Irish subjects. The principal fault of
the writer is that his views are rather too
Irish, as he sometimes commends his country-
men for virtues of temperament and conduct
which other people will be disposed to regard
as vices and weaknesses. Their freedom from
the errors and mistakes of modern thought,
for which he praises them, is part of their want
of participation in nearly every form of
modern ment'al activity, and whetfier this, in
its general effect, may be regarded as a loss or
a gain to the people generally, there can
scarcely be any difference of opinion outside
of Ireland. Taken altogether, the Contem-
porary may this month be emphatically de-
clared a good number.

The Fortnightly .Review. (Chapman and
Hall.)

Mr. Harrison's admirable article is treated '
at length elsewhere, but it is right we should
say here that the rest of the number is, upon
the whole, rather above than below the average.
Certain of the papers we have merely dipped
into, and refrain, therefore, from pronouncing
on them in the usual off-hand style. "Virgilius
the Enchanter," is a notice:of a curious book in
which the life and doings of Virgil are dis-
played as they appeared to the eyes of our
superstitious ancestors. - The contents of this
old volume, which it is the object of Mr.
Mat Culinan to make known to modern readers,
are pretty well explained by the title page.
"This booke, troatoth of the lyfe. of Virgilius,
and of his cloth, and many marvayles that he
dyd in his lyfe tyme by Whycherafte and
negramancy through the helpe of the devyls of
hell." Mr. Culinan's article is worth read-
ing, and will be relished by those who have a taste
for retrospective reviews. Mr. Edward Dow-
den's sketch of" Pieter De Laredo" is in-
teresting; but why not have pity On working
men, who are not adepts in French, and attempt
translations of illustrative poetic passages? Of
course it might ilot be an easy task, but could
it be accomplished it would add greatly to the
general reader's interest. Emilio Castelar's
article on the "Republican governent in
Europe," is not finished, but it is instructive;
and it may be added that the style is pleasant
and readable, though his estimate of seine of
his characters can scarcely be regarded as
correct. For the rest we refer the reader to
the articles themselves, simply intimating that
Mr. Trollope's instalment of his story carries
with it more than its ordinary interest.

DEMONSTRATION AT BRADFORD.

Tho members of the Trades Unions in Bradford
held a demonstration on Saturday against the
Criminal Law Amendment Acts The proceedings,
in spite of the extremely unfavourable state of the
weather, were of a very imposing character; and
a great amount of interest was manifested in them
by the inhabitants of the town. As early as two
o'clock, although rain was falling with steady
and disheartening persistence, the streets began to
be thronged with crowds of people, who had come
to witness the sight; Well-street (whence the pro-
cession was to start), Kirkgato, and Westgate
especially were lined on each side with a vast
concourse of spectators. The Trades •Unionists
mustered in great force. The purpose of the de-
monstration, as stated by largo placards and small
handbills, was to protest against the operation of
the Criminal Law Amendment Ace; and if the
number of men who took part in it be any
criterion of its success, the promoters have
nothing to desire on that score. Thirty-two
societies, having an aggiegate of 4,500 financial
members, wore represented. The Bradford societies
were the following :—Skop and Basket Makera,
Twisters and Loomors, Engineers (3
,branches)
Tinplate Workers, Cioggere, Plummbrs, Hammer-
men, Bricklayers, Stonemaaons (Bradford and
Shipley Lodges), Stonemasdne Labourers, Dray-
men, Coopers,- Tailors, Steam Sawyers, Board
and Case Makers, Iron Founders, Core Makers,
Iron Dressers, Boiler Makers, Letter:press Printer,
Coaehmakers, Warp Dressers, Amalgamated Car-
penters and Joiners, Dyers (five branches), House
Painters, Plasterers, and Plasterers' Labourers. In
addition to the foregoingthe procession was augmen-
ted by trades unionists from Leeds, Halifax, Dews-
bury, Bingloy, &nein), Idle, Itawdon, and Other
places. The procession was headed by the Gene-
ral Committee, and immediately after them came
the Wyke brass band and the Valley Dyeworks
brass band. Ten other bands—viz., the Idle,
Reelesbill, Thornton, Great Horton, Saltaire, 3rd
West York, Stanningley, Bramley, and Bowling
Artillery brass bands, and the 3rd West York
Dram and Fife Band, also took part in the pro-
cession. There was a good display of banners,
some of which were of a splendid and costly

description, -with mottoes such as—" Union with
liberty," "AU men are brethren," "Justice to
thy fellow-man," " England expects every man to
do his duty," and" Union.is strength." By far the
most pleasing and-characteristic portion of the
procession was that of the 'stonemasons, who were
present in large number* and who wore now
• leather aprons tied with blue riband, and in many
instances trimmed with ribands, and decorated

with the insignia of the mason's craft; nearly all
of them also wore white rosettes in their button-
holes. The dyers were preceded by a man riding
on horseback, and dressed in the uniform of a
general of the time of George IL; but there was
a remarkable incongruity in his bat, which, instead
of being a flat three-cornered one, was an upright,
cocked hat, such as is worn by army surgeons and
field officers of the present day. The dyers and
the painters presented a very pleasing sight, as
every person under their banner were a red
geranium on a green leaf in the button-hole of his
coat, and the effect was remarkably good. It was
easy to see, however, that a strong feeling of re-
gret existed both amongst those who came to be
seen and those who had come to see; and there is
no doubt that, had the weather been more pro-
pitious, the sight would have been vastly more
imposing. As it was, in tho faoe of the continual
downfall of rain the demonstration had a narrow
escape of becoming utterly ridiculous, both in
point of numbers and in the uncomfortable and
dejected aspect of those who had determined to
make the best of a bad bargain and carry out the
programme at any Oft. Tlae arrangements, which
were under the superintendence of a marsha
and four deputy-marshals, were very good, con-
sidering the state of the weather; and, with the
exception of one or two trifling delays in getting
the different sections into their proper places, the
procession passed off remarkably well. It was
nearly four o'clock when the procession began to
move, and the route WWI as follows ell-street,
Itirkgate, Westgate, Lumb-lano,
ilalifleld-
road, Manningliam-lano, Manor-row, Obeapsithb
Market-street, Manehoster-road,Croft-street, York-
street, Wakefield-road, Dryden-street, to the
Pair-ground, where it arrived a little before six
o'clock. A temporary platform had been erected,
and as the weather began to show some
signs of clearing up, it was determined to proceed
with the meeting which had been announced to be
held. The Mayor of Bradford (Mr. M. W.
Thompson) arrived ou the ground at about the
liinie time Ka the Preeueiell, wad he took the chair.

He was accompanied on the platform by Mr.
George Potter, Mr. John Seholefield, Mr. Norton,
. .
Mr. Conway, Mr. Guile, and Mr. Howell; of
London.; Mr. Liebman, Mr. • Galloway, Mr. Bigg,
Mr. Dalton, Mr. niddiougb, Mr. Wallwork, and
other gentlemen.
The Chairman, in the course of his opening re-
marks, gave the reason for his taking the chair at
a meeting of trade societies. He. said that he be-
lieved that if a large number of ratepayers were
anxious to have any laws repealed which they
thought unfair to them, they had a right to ask
the Mayor of the town to preside over the meeting.
It was in consequence of that he was present. He
would not say -whether he sympathised with them
or not; very likely if they were to come to close
quarters he should ask them a good Many, questions,
ttncl they would ask him some, and they might
come to some agreement which viould be satisfae.
tory to both parties. (Applause.) He then called
upon

Mr. Norton -to propose the first resolution,
which was as follows

That this meeting, having seen the unjust
prosecutions that have taken place under the
provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act,
urges upon Parliament to at -once repeal the said
Act, believing it to be totally one-sided and unjust,
being specially directed against trades unionists,
who are prejudged by its provisions with harbour-
ing criminal intentions, and pledges itself to use
every legal and constitutional means to obtain the
entire erasure from the Statute Book .of snch a
piece of unjustifiable and class legislation.

Mr. Conway seconded.
Mr. Irowoll, in supporting the resolution, said
that it dealt with two phases of the question; first,
there was what was called the preaticar objec-
ton to the Criminal Law Amendment Act; and,
secondly, what was termed the "sentimental
grievance" complained of by trades unionists.
Ile went in for the total repeal of the Act.
Thirty-five prosecutions had taken place since the
Act was passed; and if those prosecutions were
analysed it would be found that there were only
seven of them that were not ,connected with one
particular thing—that which referred to •the
system of watching works, known to workmen as
picketing." He would say, what had been said
over and over again, that workmen never
demanded the power to make disturbances, or to
do violence either to the persons or to the property
of any parties to whom they were opposed ; but
they claimed a right to go to the works and to
stand in the public highways for the purpose of
speaking peaceably and legally to those men who
came to supplant them, and to request them for their
own sake and for the sake of those who Were fight-
ing the battles of labour, not to come in and supplant
them. (Hear, hear.) After some further remarks
, the speaker concluded by pointing out that the
actual operation of that law amounted to the
feet that the employers of non-unionists had a
right to compel men against their will to work
with certain other workmen whether they were
pleased with them or not. (Applause).
Mr. D. Guile also supported the resolution. Ho
much admired the action which bad been taken at
Bradford. It showed that they were determined
in what they asked for. (Applause.) The reso-
lution which had been moved and seconded
definitely suggested several things; one was
special legislation ; another was, prosecution under
that legislation; and another was, prosecutions
directed solely to one class of men. Ho said the
time had come when all class legislation ought to
cease. (Hear, bear.) In speaking of the Criminal
Law Amendment Act, he said that it was a thing
that was unbearable, and that it only wanted a few
more demonstrations such as the one they were
now holding to. knock it on the head. Speaking of
trades unions, he said they had been formed for
the purpose of improving the conditition of the
working classes ; and he asked the employers in
Bradford whether it was not a fact that, as the
labourer had progressed, improved his :condition,
been better clothed, better fed and better housed,
the condition and position of employers had not
risen in a like ratio ? It was the mass of the
people who were boring all the other classes
upwards; and the higher the mass of the people
were raised the higher the employers were raised
also. He then dwelt at some length on the
statistical aspect of the constitution of the
House of Commons, and showed that it was
useless to expect that such a legislative body would
ever repeal the let. Parliament would have

to be dissolved, and they would have to
elect another Parliament before it was re-
pealed. In conclusion he exhorted them
to take politics out of their mouths, come
down to their social order, look to their families
and to their interest; and they would find, from
the lowest agriculttual labourer to the highest
artisan, that power was in their hands. Parlia-
ment might monopolise it a little longer, and
Might faidetwoui by milting, acre tring, and

promising, and ono thing or another, to retain it;
but the working men all over the country had
detsrmined that class legislation should cease, and
that meeting was the best testimony of that fact.
(Applause).
Mr. G-. Potter supported the resolution in an
able speech, which was much applauded.
The motion was then put and carried unani-
mously.
Mr. Dalton proposed the second resolution, Ivhieh
was as follows :---

"That this meeting considers the truck system,
as carried on in many trades throughout the
country, prejudicial to the interests of the working
classes ;- and nothing -short of its entire abolition,
pure and simple, will or can prove satisfactory."
Ridtliongh seconded, and Mr. Potter sup-
ported, this resolution, and it was 'carried unani-
mously.
_

Mr. Rigg proposed, -411 r. Galloway seconded,
and Mr. Lishman supported the third resolution,
which was as follows :

" That copies of the foregoing resolutions,
signed by the chairman, be forwarded to the
borough and county members."
Carried unanimously.
A vote of thanks to the Mayor for his kindness
in presiding on the occasion was proposed by Mr.
Potter, seconded, and passed; after which his
Worship responded, and the meeting terminated
at a littlo before eight o'clock.

THE 13IRHINOHAM TRADES.

On Saturday, a deputation from the Birmingham
Trades Council waited on Mr. P. IL Muntz,
ALP., at hia warehouse, in Great Charles-street,
to seek for the hon. gentleman's suppoit of Mr.
Vernon Harcourt's proposed .modification of the
Criminal Law Amendment Act. The deputation
consisted of Messrs. Gilliver, Gibe, Haddleton,
and Hodges, members of the Trades Council; Mr.
E. Parker, coaclunaker ; Messrs. Williams and
Osborne, plasterers; and Messrs. Bowerman and
Edwards, gunmakers.
Mr. Giles stated the object of the deputation in
seeking for the interview. He said that they
deprecated as much as anyone any resort to
violence or intimidation to coerce men to fall in
with the views of trades unions, but they strongly
objected to even a friendly conversation, with a
view to induce a man to take a certain coarse,
being construed into a punishable offence. They
thought it very unjust to them. ,They maintained
that no other portion of the community were
liable to such insulting precautions as might be
instituted under the Act, and they asked for Mr.
Muntz's assistance in supporting Mr. Vernon
Harcourt in his ondeavonr to, amend it.

Mr. Muntz said if they wished him to give an
answer on the subject of Mr. Vernon Harcourt's
.measure, he could give it at once: He believed
there was not the smallest chance of that Bill,
oven if it came to a debate, ever passing into law.
They were perfectly well aware, that it was a
private member's Bill, and even if unopposed,
they could not get it through the House without
the support of the Government. There was no
doubt, however, that the measure would meet with
a very strong opposition. He remembered very
well when the subject was originally before Par-
liament, it was sent to the House of Lords, making
it an offence for any two or more persons to weal or
beset any house or other places where men were at
work. As he understood the matter, they were all
agreed that, acting as trades unionists, as they had a
perfect right to do, arranging for strikes if they
pleased, they ought to be able to claim not to be
interfered with in any way except where threats or
violence were used. He said, without the
slightest hesitation, that he would support a
measure founded upon that principle. (Hear,
bear). At the same he claimed that any man had
a right to work where he liked; but they also were
perfectly right, by conversation and argument, and
friendly intercourse, to persuade that man into
their way of thinking. He agreed that trade
unions were far better managed than they were
twenty years ago, and they rarely heard of such
acts as those done by the brickrnakers at Man-
chester, or the workmen in some trades at Sheffield.
The best thing for them to do was to explain to Mr.
Bruce the necessity for this change. They might
believe it or not, but it was only by a Government
measure that they had any chanoe of success. He
should be happy to assist them, though he did
not much care about going to Ministers, not
being a particular favourite in those quarters.

THE LEEDS 'ENGINEERING TRADE
AND ZYZT.EMATIC oVEITY.II.E.

A public meeting of the engineering trade of
Leeds, to discuss the question of systematic over-
time, was held on Saturday afternoon, in the
Circus, Cookridge-street. The atteadance Wee

large.
Mr. Councillor Child, who presided, spoke
strongly against the practice of systematic over-
time, which, he said, prevented working men from
paying proper attention to their wives and families,
to the improvement of their intellect and their
physical health.
Mr.. J. Naylor, pattern maker, moved the first
resolution as follows :
" That this meeting, having carefully considered
the evils resulting from the working of eystemstie
overtime, and seeing that it prevents the phy!ieeir
social, and intellectual improvement so essential to
those employed in tbe iron trade, hereby Pledges
itself to take such steps as will either greatly cur-
tail it or otherwise abolish it entirely."
Mr. Langstaff, mechanic, seconded the resolu-
tion, which was unanimously carried.
The second resolution, which demanded that
when overtime was worked time and a half be
charged for the first two hours, and double time
afterwards, and that each day stand for itialt; wAs
moved by Mr. B. Jordan, smith, and seconded 11
Mr. W. Nicholson, ironfounder.
Mr. Luke Hope moved as an amendment that
time and a quarter be clArged for the first two
hours, time and a half for the second two hours,
and double, time for tho remainder of the night,
and Sundays, Good Fridays, and Christinas=days
(each day to stand for itself).
• The amendment having been seconded, a short
discusaion followed, during which strong opinions
were expressed that systematic overtime slot"
altogether be abolished.
On the vote being taken, the original reulutioa
was carried by a large majority.
It was next resolved that a circular, embodying
the above resolution, be sent to all the employers
in the engineering and ironfounding trades in

Leeds.
The meeting separated with a vote of thanks tA)
the chairman.

In the Bail Court, Westminster., on Thursday,
before Justices Blackburn, Mellor, and Lush, the
case of the Queen v. the Registrar of Friendly So-
cieties came on for hearing. A rule had been
obtained by the Executive Council of the Anitagamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners- 412
London calling upon Mr. Stevenson, the regis-
trar of friendly societies, and Mr. Fryer and Mr.
Thompson, members of the General Council in
Manchebter, to show cause why, a mandamus
should not issue commanding Mr. Stevenson to
register that branch of the Society in the name of
"The Amalgamated Society of Carpenters 15101
Joiners." The Society comprised 242 branches,
with an executive eouncil in London of seven
members, and a general council in Manchester of
10 members. The funds were left in the hands of
each particular branch, and each distributed its
own funds, subject to this, that if great distress
happened in any district the more prosperous
districts contributed to the funds of the former.
On the 18th March, 1871, a difference era°
between the Executive and the General Councils,
when the Executive Council took forcible possesion of the books and propev,ty within their parr
belonging to the Society, but the branches wore
able to retain their funds. After- that An expos'
sion of opinion of the Society was taken, which
resulted in 222 branches out of the 242 supporting
the General Council. Of the funds £21,916 folloW
the General Council and only £3,115 the Exeou-
tive Council; and out of 10,000 members but
1,300 supported the latter. This Society being
in restraint of trade, they were only able to regis-
ter their rules for the purpose of settling differences
that might arise between them. On the 29th
June, 1871, some weeks after the separation, the
Trade Union Act passed, whereby it was enacted
that no trade union could be registered under a
name identical with that of another, or so near the
name as to be likely to deceive the public. On the
sth of August both parties applied to be registered
separately in the name of the Amalgatnated
Society of Carpenters and Joiners, and in con-
sequence of that enactment Mr. Stevenson refused
to comply with the request. On the Bth December,
1871, the Secretary of State for the Home Depart-
ment issued rules under the Trade Union Act, elle
of which was that the Registrar should not registor.
a trade union under a name identical with thet or
any existing trade union known to him, whether
reeisterad or not, or so resembling the name se
likay to deceive the public. On the 23rd Deem-
bar the Executive Council, and on the aOttil
Dec-mber the General Council renewed ttri_t,
plications for registration in the same napr,
Mr, Stevenson again declined to milder inner
Jraq2

Mr. Henry Jqaos, Q.C., and Mr. Bexley,
showed cause against the rule, and Mr. Macdonald
supported it. •
Mr. James contended that the Registrar had
acted rightly, as both under the clause of the
Act and the rules issued by the Homo Secretary
ho was bound to refuse registration under the
circumstances. Ile was ready to let the matter
stand as it was, but if the Executive Council
wished to'beregustered, they Must alter, however
slightly, the name of the Society. If they were
to be registered in the identical name of the old
Society, they would be able to claim the whole of
the funds. There could 'be no doubt that it was
an attempt on the part of the Executive Council
to snap at the funds by means of registration,
Mr. M‘Donald, in support of the rule, contended
that the Registrar had ncr power to refuse to
register therExcentive• Council as the original
Society, and that the rules made by the Home
gecrotary were in excess of his authority, as they
imposed upon the Registrar, who was merely an
executive officer, the ditty —of importing his own
personal knowledge into the matter.
• Mr. Justice Blackburn said there was no real
hardship in the case. All the' parties had to do
was to make a slight alteration in the name of the
Society, and then they would be entitled to regis-
tration. This Court had nothing to do with the
merits of tha case, and for that they must refer
them to Chancery. The Registrar had properly
exorcised his jurtediction, and the Court would
not interfere. After hearing the arguments the
Court discharged the rule.

articles.title: LABOUR REPRESENTATION LEAGUE.
articles.text:
THE LABOUR REPRESENTATION
LEAGUE.

At the usual meeting of the council, held
at '2l, Oickspur-street, on Friday last, thci
present aspect_ of political parties was dis-
cussed, in relation to their action as it affects
the labouring population. , great dissatisfac-
tion was expressed by those present at the
meagre progress made in Parliament with
measures deeply concerning the interests of
thousands of our countrymen and women,
whose prostrate condition renders them unable
to assist themselves. The measures'. particu-
larised were-4—The Mines' Regt}lation, the
Truck, and the Criminal Law Aniendment
Bills, now all of them before the House of
Commons, which, when taken with the defeats
of the clause relieving egndidates_from official
expenses at eleetkins; and of Mr. V. Harcourt's
Bill for registering voters, exposes a great
amount of indifference on the part of a
majority of the House to the interests of
labour.
The following resolution was submitted :
"That, upon observing the dilatory conduct
of Parliament in dealing with measures vitally
affecting large numbers of the working classes,
it is the opinion of this League that steps
should be immediately taken, prior to the
dissolution, to place before the constituencies
as candidates for election to Parliament
artizans who understand and can represent
the opinions of their order."
Especially is this made requisite as the
defeat, at Oldham, of a friend to labour (al-
though coming from another grade of society)
renders it imperative upon the masses, if they
must meet defeat, to accept it in themselves,
upon their own platform, and upon their own
issues.

This was supported by Messrs. Baker,
Savage, Brighty, and Campin, and carried
unanimously.
The council afterwards arranged the order
of the debates at the Century Club, Pall Mall.
Ist, On Charitable Endowments; 2nd, The
Hours of Labour; 3rd, Land and its Tenures;
4th, Purchase of Railways by the State; sth,
Disestablishmeut of the English Church; 6th,
Personal Representation. -Walter Morrison,
Esq., M.P., will preside on Friday! June 14th,
when Thomas Hare, Esq., barrister-at-law,
will road the first paper on Charitable Endow-
ments.
